doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

title: What makes a good melody: singability and ideas in the universe
summary: She writes by singing lines and describes the Elizabeth Gilbert idea that ideas wait to be caught; Rowe quotes Karl Berger.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: and they used – the critics used the term “melodic” and “melodies.” And what makes a good melody for you?

Ooo. That’s a great question. I suppose something singable, and in fact a lot of the time when I’m writing I’m singing the line rather than necessarily playing it on the piano or the saxophone. Or I might start there and then I think oh well what comes next. Or sing what I’ve just written and then see what voice comes up then. So I suppose that’s part of it. Being singable. But it’s so intangible, some of this stuff, the quest for the perfect melody. I will answer that from a spiritual perspective actually, because I love this concept that I also discovered from the writer Elizabeth Gilbert, who I think is a great speaker as well. She’s very articulate and she’s got some very interesting ideas about creativity. And one of those, I don’t think it’s her idea but she adheres to this idea, that ideas are present in the universe. We can’t see them because they’re in a different dimension, but they’re constantly inviting us to interact with them and come and play. And sometimes when we’re open enough we get to have a relationship with that idea and we catch it and we write it down. And I just thought, oh that’s so interesting and so different from this idea that everything comes from the individual. You have to come up with everything and it’s all on your shoulders and the responsibility comes from you, so if it’s not very good, you’re not very good. It’s very liberating in that sense. But I really like it, just when I’m writing, especially when it’s the more melodic pieces, but the idea is out there, and I’ve just got to keep listening until I can harness it. And that for me is where the most satisfying writing becomes, because it’s almost like it’s inevitable, because the melody already exists and I’ve just written it down, even though it doesn’t exist because obviously that would be plagiarism. So it’s coming from me but it’s not, it’s sort of in there somewhere, in a different dimension, I’m trying to find it. And it’s quite good. Many people would just be – many people might be at this moment thinking what is she all about, this mad English woman. But you know --

Well Karl Berger, who passed away a couple of years ago, but he had the Creative Music Workshop north of New York. And he said, “Music is being thought of as something that entertains us and that can be used for other certain purposes. But it’s a world. You go there. Everybody can go there whether you play or not. You’re in the world of spontaneity and you’re no longer in the thinking world. You leave the thinking world behind.
